justice: The street gives substantial space to motor movement on a wide paved carriageway, but there is no clearly designated sidewalk on either side, so pedestrian space is not evenly allocated.
Rolled curbs along the edge and a mostly level road surface help general access, but there are no visible tactile paving strips, marked crossings, or dedicated barrier-free pedestrian zones.
A handcart and scattered items placed at the building edge intrude into the already ambiguous walking area, indicating that rules protecting non-motorized users are weak or unenforced.
safety: The lane is relatively narrow and appears low-speed, with very light traffic and good forward visibility, which reduces crash risk for all users.
There is no painted centerline, crosswalk, bike lane, or pedestrian refuge, so movement relies on informal negotiation rather than explicit safety design.

Streetlights are present on the right side, which supports nighttime safety, but overhead utility wires and the lack of clear separation between walkers, cyclists, and vehicles weaken overall safety performance.
livability: The planted edge with shrubs and street trees adds greenery and softens the corridor, supporting a more pleasant residential environment.
The street appears quiet and low in traffic, which can support calm daily living, but there are very few visible social amenities such as benches, shops, or gathering spaces.
Blank residential walls, garage-style frontage, and limited visible pedestrian activity reduce street vitality and everyday interaction.
sustainability: Trees and shrub planting along the right side provide some green infrastructure and ecological value compared with a fully hardscaped street.
The simple narrow local street and low traffic environment may discourage high-speed driving and imply lower transport intensity than a major road.
However, there is no visible bike lane, bus stop, permeable paving, bioswale, or stormwater feature, so support for low-carbon mobility and water-sensitive design remains limited.
aesthetics: The green verge with shrubs, trimmed planting, and evenly spaced street trees improves visual quality and creates a softer edge.
The street is visually coherent with a long straight perspective and relatively tidy paving, giving a simple and orderly appearance.
Aesthetic quality is reduced by exposed overhead cables, the utilitarian building facade with barred windows and roller shutter, and the handcart and scattered objects in the foreground.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderate to low because the deciduous trees are mostly leafless and provide little effective shade at the time shown.
Physical comfort is limited by the absence of a clear sidewalk, benches, or dedicated resting areas, even though the road surface itself appears fairly smooth and level.
Psychological comfort benefits from the quiet setting, low visible traffic, and open sightlines, but the lack of protected pedestrian space can make walking feel exposed.
walkability: Walkability is weakened because there is no continuous, clearly marked sidewalk; pedestrians would likely have to share the carriageway or walk along narrow edges.
The roadway surface looks flat and unobstructed for much of the corridor, which helps basic walking movement, but the handcart and frontage clutter reduce edge usability.
There are no visible crossings, curb ramps at intersections, active frontages, or pedestrian wayfinding elements to support convenient and attractive walking.
bikeability: The low-traffic, low-speed character of the street may make casual cycling possible, especially for experienced riders on a local road.
There is no dedicated bike lane, protective separation, bicycle markings, or intersection treatment, so cycling conditions depend entirely on sharing space with other users.
No bicycle parking, repair facilities, or cycling-oriented signage are visible, limiting convenience and network legibility for cyclists.
